title: Japanese grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Japanese, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is natural standard Japanese, polite at first and casual later, written the way Japanese people write it, with its reading in rōmaji (Latin letters).

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name, where you're from and what you do: your first Japanese conversation.
lessons.topic: {{XはYです|X wa Y desu}}; leaving out “I”; {{さん|san}}

goal.t: はじめまして。サラです。よろしくお願いします。
goal.r: Hajimemashite. Sara desu. Yoroshiku onegaishimasu.
goal.tr: How do you do? I'm Sarah. Nice to meet you.

dialog.t: はじめまして。田中です。
dialog.r: Hajimemashite. Tanaka desu.
dialog.tr: How do you do? I'm Tanaka.

dialog.t: はじめまして。サラです。アメリカ人です。
dialog.r: Hajimemashite. Sara desu. Amerikajin desu.
dialog.tr: How do you do? I'm Sarah. I'm American.

dialog.t: 私は会社員です。
dialog.r: Watashi wa kaishain desu.
dialog.tr: I work for a company.

dialog.t: 私は学生です。
dialog.r: Watashi wa gakusei desu.
dialog.tr: I'm a student.

dialog.t: よろしくお願いします。
dialog.r: Yoroshiku onegaishimasu.
dialog.tr: Nice to meet you.

dialog.t: こちらこそ、よろしくお願いします。
dialog.r: Kochira koso, yoroshiku onegaishimasu.
dialog.tr: Nice to meet you too.

blocks.p: Look at the shape of the sentences: a word, then {{です|desu}}. {{サラです|Sara desu}} is “(I) am Sarah”. {{です|desu}} does the job of “am, is, are”, and it comes at the **end** of the sentence: in Japanese, the word that holds the sentence together always comes last.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm a student.

blocks.p: **Saying who you're talking about.** {{私は学生です|Watashi wa gakusei desu}} is, word for word, “me, as for, student, am”: “As for me, I'm a student.” {{私|watashi}} is “I”, and {{は|wa}} after it marks what the sentence is about. This little word is written with the letter normally read “ha”, but as a grammar word it is always said **wa**.

blocks.means: a little word that goes after a word to show its job in the sentence. Japanese has several: {{は|wa}}, {{の|no}}, {{を|o}}…
what a sentence is about (“as for me…”). In Japanese it is marked with the particle {{は|wa}}.

blocks.p: **Leave out “I”.** Once it's clear who you mean, Japanese drops it. Mr Tanaka just says {{田中です|Tanaka desu}}, “(I'm) Tanaka”. Saying {{私は|watashi wa}} in every sentence sounds heavy: use it when you turn to talk about yourself, as he does when he says what he does.

table: for anyone, man or woman, polite
Mr / Ms Tanaka: for other people, never yourself

blocks.p: **{{さん|san}}.** Put {{さん|san}} after other people's names: {{田中さん|Tanaka-san}}, {{サラさん|Sara-san}}. It works for men and women, with first names or family names, like Mr and Ms. Never put it after your own name. And there is no “a” or “the”, and no plural: {{学生です|gakusei desu}} can be “I'm a student” or “We're students”.

ex.t: 私はサラです。
ex.r: Watashi wa Sara desu.
ex.tr: I'm Sarah.

ex.t: 学生です。
ex.r: Gakusei desu.
ex.tr: I'm a student.
ex.note: no “I”: it's clear who

ex.t: 私は日本人です。
ex.r: Watashi wa Nihonjin desu.
ex.tr: I'm Japanese.
ex.note: country + {{人|jin}} “person”: {{アメリカ人|Amerikajin}}, {{イギリス人|Igirisujin}}

ex.t: 田中さんは先生です。
ex.r: Tanaka-san wa sensei desu.
ex.tr: Mr Tanaka is a teacher.
ex.note: the same shape for anyone: nothing changes for he or she

ex.t: マリアさんはメキシコ人です。
ex.r: Maria-san wa Mekishikojin desu.
ex.tr: Maria is Mexican.

ex.t: 会社員です。
ex.r: Kaishain desu.
ex.tr: I work for a company.
ex.note: word for word “(I'm) a company employee”: the usual way to say you have an office job

blocks.tip: Japanese is written with three kinds of characters, mixed in one sentence: **hiragana** (は, で, す…) for grammar words and endings, **katakana** (サ, ラ…) for foreign names and words such as {{アメリカ|Amerika}}, and **kanji** (私, 学生…), characters from Chinese, for the main words. There are no spaces between words. You don't need to read any of it yet: every example has its reading in Latin letters (rōmaji), and tapping it lets you hear it. Learning hiragana soon will make everything easier.

mistakes.why: {{さん|san}} shows respect to other people: never put it after your own name. {{私はサラです。|Watashi wa Sara desu.}}
The topic particle is said “wa” but written {{は|wa}}, not {{わ|wa}}.

lessons.title: Ask yes-or-no questions and say “not”
lessons.summary: Turn any sentence into a question with one little word, answer yes or no, and say what you're not: “Are you a student?” “No, I'm not.”
lessons.topic: {{か|ka}} for questions; {{はい|hai}} and {{いいえ|iie}}; {{じゃありません|ja arimasen}}; {{も|mo}} “too”

goal.t: いいえ、学生じゃありません。会社員です。
goal.r: Iie, gakusei ja arimasen. Kaishain desu.
goal.tr: No, I'm not a student. I work for a company.

dialog.t: すみません、アメリカ人ですか。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, Amerikajin desu ka.
dialog.tr: Excuse me, are you American?

dialog.t: いいえ、アメリカ人じゃありません。イギリス人です。
dialog.r: Iie, Amerikajin ja arimasen. Igirisujin desu.
dialog.tr: No, I'm not American. I'm British.

dialog.t: そうですか。学生ですか。
dialog.r: Sō desu ka. Gakusei desu ka.
dialog.tr: I see. Are you a student?

dialog.t: はい、そうです。ゆいさんも学生ですか。
dialog.r: Hai, sō desu. Yui-san mo gakusei desu ka.
dialog.tr: Yes, I am. Are you a student too, Yui?

dialog.t: はい、私も学生です。
dialog.r: Hai, watashi mo gakusei desu.
dialog.tr: Yes, I'm a student too.

blocks.p: **Questions: add {{か|ka}}.** Put {{か|ka}} at the end of a sentence and it becomes a question. Nothing else moves: {{学生です。|Gakusei desu.}} “I'm a student.” → {{学生ですか。|Gakusei desu ka.}} “Are you a student?” Your voice goes up on {{か|ka}}. In writing, a question with {{か|ka}} usually ends with the Japanese full stop {{。}}.

blocks.means: the form of a sentence that says “not”: I'm not, she doesn't.

table: {{学生じゃありません。|Gakusei ja arimasen.}}

blocks.p: **Yes and no.** {{はい|hai}} is “yes”, {{いいえ|iie}} “no”. “Yes, I am” or “Yes, that's right” is {{はい、そうです|hai, sō desu}}. For “not”, put {{じゃありません|ja arimasen}} in the place of {{です|desu}}. You will also see {{ではありません|dewa arimasen}}: the same, a little more formal, and usual in writing.

**{{も|mo}} “too”.** Put {{も|mo}} in the place of {{は|wa}}: {{私は学生です|Watashi wa gakusei desu}} “I'm a student” → {{私も学生です|watashi mo gakusei desu}} “I'm a student too”. {{も|mo}} takes over the job of {{は|wa}}, so the two never come together.

ex.t: 先生ですか。
ex.r: Sensei desu ka.
ex.tr: Are you a teacher?

ex.t: はい、そうです。
ex.r: Hai, sō desu.
ex.tr: Yes, I am.
ex.note: word for word “yes, that's so”

ex.t: いいえ、先生じゃありません。
ex.r: Iie, sensei ja arimasen.
ex.tr: No, I'm not a teacher.

ex.t: 田中さんは日本人ですか。
ex.r: Tanaka-san wa Nihonjin desu ka.
ex.tr: Is Mr Tanaka Japanese?

ex.t: マリアさんも学生です。
ex.r: Maria-san mo gakusei desu.
ex.tr: Maria is a student too.

ex.t: 私はアメリカ人じゃありません。カナダ人です。
ex.r: Watashi wa Amerikajin ja arimasen. Kanadajin desu.
ex.tr: I'm not American. I'm Canadian.

blocks.tip: {{そうですか。|Sō desu ka.}}, said with a falling voice, means “I see” or “Oh, really?”. Japanese people say it all the time to show they're listening: it isn't a question at all.

mistakes.why: {{も|mo}} takes the place of {{は|wa}}: never both. {{私も学生です。|Watashi mo gakusei desu.}}

mistakes.wrong: 学生じゃありませんです。
mistakes.why: {{じゃありません|ja arimasen}} replaces {{です|desu}}: nothing is added after it.

lessons.title: Point at things and ask what they are
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?”, tell “this” from “that” and “that over there”, and say whose something is: “It's my bag.”
lessons.topic: {{これ|kore}}, {{それ|sore}}, {{あれ|are}}; {{何|nan}} “what”; {{の|no}} “my, of”

goal.t: すみません、これは何ですか。
goal.r: Sumimasen, kore wa nan desu ka.
goal.tr: Excuse me, what's this?

dialog.t: すみません、これは何ですか。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, kore wa nan desu ka.
dialog.tr: Excuse me, what's this?

dialog.t: それはおにぎりです。
dialog.r: Sore wa onigiri desu.
dialog.tr: That's an onigiri, a rice ball.

dialog.t: あれもおにぎりですか。
dialog.r: Are mo onigiri desu ka.
dialog.tr: Is that one over there an onigiri too?

dialog.t: いいえ、あれはお餅です。
dialog.r: Iie, are wa omochi desu.
dialog.tr: No, that's mochi, a rice cake.

blocks.p: **This, that, and that over there.** Japanese has three words where English has two, and the choice depends on where the thing is:
So the shop assistant answers {{これは何ですか|kore wa nan desu ka}} with {{それは…|sore wa …}}: the thing is near you, so for them it's “that”.

**What?** {{何|nan}} “what” goes exactly where the answer will go: {{これは何ですか。|Kore wa nan desu ka.}} “What's this?” → {{これはお茶です。|Kore wa ocha desu.}} “This is tea.” No words change places, as they do in English: put {{何|nan}} in the gap and {{か|ka}} at the end. ({{何|nan}} is said “nan” before {{です|desu}}, and “nani” in many other places.)

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing, a place or an idea: student, tea, Tokyo, music.

blocks.p: **{{の|no}}: my, your, of.** {{の|no}} joins two nouns, and the first tells you more about the second: {{私のかばん|watashi no kaban}} “my bag”, {{田中さんの車|Tanaka-san no kuruma}} “Mr Tanaka's car”, {{日本の車|Nihon no kuruma}} “a Japanese car”, {{日本語の先生|Nihongo no sensei}} “a Japanese teacher”. The owner comes first, as with English 's. {{だれの|dare no}} is “whose”.

ex.t: これは何ですか。
ex.r: Kore wa nan desu ka.
ex.tr: What's this?

ex.t: それは日本のお茶です。
ex.r: Sore wa Nihon no ocha desu.
ex.tr: That's Japanese tea.

ex.t: あれは私の車です。
ex.r: Are wa watashi no kuruma desu.
ex.tr: That one over there is my car.

ex.t: これはだれのかさですか。
ex.r: Kore wa dare no kasa desu ka.
ex.tr: Whose umbrella is this?

ex.t: 田中さんのです。
ex.r: Tanaka-san no desu.
ex.tr: It's Mr Tanaka's.
ex.note: {{の|no}} at the end: “Tanaka's (one)”, without saying the thing again

ex.t: 私の名前はサラです。
ex.r: Watashi no namae wa Sara desu.
ex.tr: My name is Sarah.

blocks.tip: {{お|o}} in front of some words, as in {{お茶|ocha}} “tea” and {{お餅|omochi}}, makes them sound polite and gentle. You'll hear these words with it almost always.

mistakes.why: The owner comes first, then {{の|no}}, then the thing: {{私のかばん|watashi no kaban}} “my bag”.
Two nouns side by side need {{の|no}} between them: {{私の|watashi no}} “my”.

{{これは何ですか。|Kore wa nan desu ka.}}

lessons.title: Ask for things and how much they cost
lessons.summary: Shop and order: point at what you want, ask the price, and say how many: “Two of these cakes, please.”
lessons.topic: {{この|kono}}, {{その|sono}}, {{あの|ano}}; {{をください|o kudasai}}; {{いくら|ikura}}; numbers and {{つ|tsu}}

goal.t: このケーキを二つください。
goal.r: Kono kēki o futatsu kudasai.
goal.tr: Two of these cakes, please.

dialog.t: いらっしゃいませ。
dialog.r: Irasshaimase.
dialog.tr: Welcome!

dialog.t: すみません、このパンはいくらですか。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, kono pan wa ikura desu ka.
dialog.tr: Excuse me, how much is this bread?

dialog.t: それは二百円です。
dialog.r: Sore wa nihyaku-en desu.
dialog.tr: That's two hundred yen.

dialog.t: じゃ、それを二つください。あのケーキも一つください。
dialog.r: Ja, sore o futatsu kudasai. Ano kēki mo hitotsu kudasai.
dialog.tr: Then two of those, please. And one of those cakes over there too.

dialog.t: はい。全部で八百円です。
dialog.r: Hai. Zenbu de happyaku-en desu.
dialog.tr: Certainly. That's eight hundred yen altogether.

blocks.p: **This, that + a noun.** Before a noun, “this” is {{この|kono}}, not {{これ|kore}}: {{これ|kore}} stands alone, {{この|kono}} always has a noun after it.

table: {{あのパン|ano pan}} that bread over there

blocks.p: **Asking for something: {{～をください|… o kudasai}}.** The thing, then {{を|o}}, then {{ください|kudasai}} “please give me”. {{を|o}} marks the thing you want (a later lesson says more about it); it's written with its own letter and said “o”. {{コーヒーをください。|Kōhī o kudasai.}} “A coffee, please.” In a restaurant, {{～をお願いします|… o onegaishimasu}} is just as good, and a little softer.

**How much, and how many.** {{いくらですか。|Ikura desu ka.}} “How much is it?” Prices are a number + {{円|en}} “yen”. To say how many things, use the counting words in the third column, and put them **after** {{を|o}}, just before the verb: {{それを二つください|sore o futatsu kudasai}} “two of those, please”.

Bigger numbers are built like sums: {{百|hyaku}} 100, {{千|sen}} 1,000, {{万|man}} 10,000. Japanese counts big numbers in ten-thousands, so 20,000 is {{二万|niman}}, “two ten-thousands”. A few change their sound: {{三百|sanbyaku}}, {{六百|roppyaku}}, {{八百|happyaku}}, {{三千|sanzen}}, {{八千|hassen}}. So 350 yen is {{三百五十円|sanbyaku gojū-en}}.

ex.t: コーヒーを一つください。
ex.r: Kōhī o hitotsu kudasai.
ex.tr: One coffee, please.

ex.t: このシャツはいくらですか。
ex.r: Kono shatsu wa ikura desu ka.
ex.tr: How much is this shirt?

ex.t: 三千円です。
ex.r: Sanzen-en desu.
ex.tr: It's three thousand yen.

ex.t: あのりんごを五つください。
ex.r: Ano ringo o itsutsu kudasai.
ex.tr: Five of those apples over there, please.

ex.t: お茶とおにぎりをください。
ex.r: Ocha to onigiri o kudasai.
ex.tr: Tea and a rice ball, please.
ex.note: {{と|to}} “and” joins nouns

ex.t: 水をお願いします。
ex.r: Mizu o onegaishimasu.
ex.tr: Water, please.
ex.note: in a restaurant

blocks.tip: Shop staff greet you with {{いらっしゃいませ|irasshaimase}} “welcome”. You don't answer it: a nod or a smile is enough.

mistakes.why: Before a noun, “this” is {{この|kono}}: {{このパン|kono pan}}.

mistakes.wrong: 二つのコーヒーをください。
mistakes.right: コーヒーを二つください。
mistakes.why: When you order, the number goes after {{を|o}}, just before the verb: {{コーヒーを二つください。|Kōhī o futatsu kudasai.}} The other order is possible, but sounds stiff.

practice.tr: How much is this cake?
practice.why: Before a noun: {{この|kono}}. {{このケーキはいくらですか。|Kono kēki wa ikura desu ka.}}

options: コーヒーとケーキをお願いします。

practice.why: {{あのかばんはいくらですか。|Ano kaban wa ikura desu ka.}}

lessons.title: Say what you do, and what you don't
lessons.summary: Talk about everyday actions, what you eat, drink, watch and study, and what you don't: “I drink coffee every morning.”
lessons.topic: verbs in {{ます|masu}} and {{ません|masen}}; {{を|o}}; the verb at the end

goal.t: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
goal.r: Maiasa kōhī o nomimasu.
goal.tr: I drink coffee every morning.

dialog.t: エマさん、肉を食べますか。
dialog.r: Ema-san, niku o tabemasu ka.
dialog.tr: Emma, do you eat meat?

dialog.t: いいえ、食べません。魚を食べます。
dialog.r: Iie, tabemasen. Sakana o tabemasu.
dialog.tr: No, I don't. I eat fish.

dialog.t: お酒を飲みますか。
dialog.r: Osake o nomimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Do you drink alcohol?

dialog.t: はい、ときどき飲みます。
dialog.r: Hai, tokidoki nomimasu.
dialog.tr: Yes, sometimes.

blocks.means: a word for an action or a state: eat, go, sleep, have.

blocks.p: **Verbs end in {{ます|masu}}.** {{食べます|tabemasu}} “eat”, {{飲みます|nomimasu}} “drink”, {{見ます|mimasu}} “watch, see”. The polite form of every verb ends in {{ます|masu}}, and it's the same whoever does it: {{私は飲みます|watashi wa nomimasu}} “I drink”, {{田中さんは飲みます|Tanaka-san wa nomimasu}} “Mr Tanaka drinks”. No endings for I, you or she to learn.

blocks.means: the person or thing an action is done to: I drink **coffee**.

blocks.p: **The object takes {{を|o}}, and the verb comes last.** Word for word, Japanese says “I coffee drink”: {{私はコーヒーを飲みます|watashi wa kōhī o nomimasu}}. {{を|o}} goes right after the object, and the verb closes the sentence. Time words usually come first: {{毎朝|maiasa}} “every morning”.

**Not: {{ません|masen}}.** Change {{ます|masu}} to {{ません|masen}}: {{飲みません|nomimasen}} “I don't drink”. Questions take {{か|ka}} as before, and the answer repeats the verb: {{食べますか。|Tabemasu ka.}} → {{はい、食べます。|Hai, tabemasu.}} or {{いいえ、食べません。|Iie, tabemasen.}}

**Now and later.** The {{ます|masu}} form covers what you do (habits) and what you will do: {{明日、映画を見ます|ashita, eiga o mimasu}} “I'll watch a movie tomorrow”. The time word tells you which. And {{します|shimasu}} “do” makes many verbs out of nouns: {{勉強します|benkyō shimasu}} “study”, {{テニスをします|tenisu o shimasu}} “play tennis”.

ex.t: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
ex.r: Maiasa kōhī o nomimasu.
ex.tr: I drink coffee every morning.

ex.t: 私は肉を食べません。
ex.r: Watashi wa niku o tabemasen.
ex.tr: I don't eat meat.

ex.t: 毎晩テレビを見ます。
ex.r: Maiban terebi o mimasu.
ex.tr: I watch TV every evening.

ex.t: 日本語を勉強します。
ex.r: Nihongo o benkyō shimasu.
ex.tr: I study Japanese.

ex.t: 明日、テニスをします。
ex.r: Ashita, tenisu o shimasu.
ex.tr: I'm going to play tennis tomorrow.
ex.note: the same form for the future

ex.t: 田中さんは新聞を読みますか。
ex.r: Tanaka-san wa shinbun o yomimasu ka.
ex.tr: Does Mr Tanaka read the newspaper?

blocks.tip: {{ときどき|tokidoki}} “sometimes”, {{よく|yoku}} “often”, {{毎日|mainichi}} “every day” go before the verb, usually near the start: {{よくテレビを見ます|yoku terebi o mimasu}} “I often watch TV”.

mistakes.wrong: 私は飲みますコーヒーを。

mistakes.why: The verb comes at the end: the object with {{を|o}}, then the verb. {{私はコーヒーを飲みます。|Watashi wa kōhī o nomimasu.}}

mistakes.wrong: 肉を食べますじゃありません。
mistakes.why: {{じゃありません|ja arimasen}} is for nouns. A verb says “not” with {{ません|masen}}: {{食べません|tabemasen}}.

lessons.title: Say where you're going, when and how
lessons.summary: Talk about going places: where to, at what time, on which day, and how you get there: “I go to work by train at eight.”
lessons.topic: {{行きます|ikimasu}}, {{来ます|kimasu}}, {{帰ります|kaerimasu}}; {{へ|e}} or {{に|ni}} “to”; {{に|ni}} with times; {{で|de}} “by”

goal.t: 毎朝八時に電車で会社へ行きます。
goal.r: Maiasa hachi-ji ni densha de kaisha e ikimasu.
goal.tr: Every morning I go to work by train at eight.

dialog.t: 週末、どこへ行きますか。
dialog.r: Shūmatsu, doko e ikimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Where are you going at the weekend?

dialog.t: 土曜日に京都へ行きます。
dialog.r: Doyōbi ni Kyōto e ikimasu.
dialog.tr: I'm going to Kyoto on Saturday.

dialog.t: いいですね。何で行きますか。
dialog.r: Ii desu ne. Nan de ikimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Nice! How are you getting there?

dialog.t: 新幹線で行きます。日曜日の夜に帰ります。
dialog.r: Shinkansen de ikimasu. Nichiyōbi no yoru ni kaerimasu.
dialog.tr: By bullet train. I'm coming back on Sunday night.

blocks.p: **Three verbs of movement.** {{行きます|ikimasu}} “go”, {{来ます|kimasu}} “come”, {{帰ります|kaerimasu}} “go back, go home”: back to where you live, your home or your country. Japanese uses {{帰ります|kaerimasu}} where English says “go home” or “come back”.

**Where to: {{へ|e}} or {{に|ni}}.** The place, then {{へ|e}} or {{に|ni}}, then the verb: {{京都へ行きます|Kyōto e ikimasu}} or {{京都に行きます|Kyōto ni ikimasu}} “I'm going to Kyoto”. Both are right. {{へ|e}}, as a particle, is said “e”. {{どこへ|doko e}} is “where to?”.

**When: {{に|ni}} with clock times and days.** {{八時に|hachi-ji ni}} “at eight”, {{土曜日に|doyōbi ni}} “on Saturday”, {{三月に|sangatsu ni}} “in March”. Words that count from today, like {{今日|kyō}} “today”, {{明日|ashita}} “tomorrow”, {{毎日|mainichi}} “every day” and {{週末|shūmatsu}} “the weekend”, take no {{に|ni}}.

**How: {{で|de}}.** The means of transport, then {{で|de}}: {{電車で|densha de}} “by train”, {{バスで|basu de}} “by bus”, {{車で|kuruma de}} “by car”. On foot is {{歩いて|aruite}} “walking”. To ask how, say {{何で|nan de}} “by what?”.

table: at what time, on what day

blocks.p: The usual order is: when, how, where to, then the verb. But the particles carry the meaning, so the order can change. Only the verb must stay last.

ex.t: 明日、東京へ行きます。
ex.r: Ashita, Tōkyō e ikimasu.
ex.tr: I'm going to Tokyo tomorrow.

ex.t: 何時に家へ帰りますか。
ex.r: Nan-ji ni ie e kaerimasu ka.
ex.tr: What time are you going home?

ex.t: 七時に帰ります。
ex.r: Shichi-ji ni kaerimasu.
ex.tr: I'll be home at seven.

ex.t: バスで学校へ行きます。
ex.r: Basu de gakkō e ikimasu.
ex.tr: I go to school by bus.

ex.t: 姉は来月日本へ来ます。
ex.r: Ane wa raigetsu Nihon e kimasu.
ex.tr: My sister is coming to Japan next month.

ex.t: 歩いて駅へ行きます。
ex.r: Aruite eki e ikimasu.
ex.tr: I walk to the station.

blocks.tip: Clock times are a number + {{時|ji}}. Watch three of them: {{四時|yo-ji}} four o'clock, {{七時|shichi-ji}} seven, {{九時|ku-ji}} nine. Half past is {{半|han}}: {{三時半|san-ji han}} “half past three”.

mistakes.wrong: 明日に東京へ行きます。
mistakes.why: {{明日|ashita}}, {{今日|kyō}} and {{毎日|mainichi}} take no {{に|ni}}: only clock times, days of the week and dates do.

mistakes.wrong: 電車に会社へ行きます。
mistakes.right: 電車で会社へ行きます。
mistakes.tr: I go to work by train.
mistakes.why: “By” train, bus or car is {{で|de}}: {{電車で|densha de}}.

lessons.title: Talk about your daily routine
lessons.summary: Say where you do things, who with, and from when until when: “I study Japanese at home every evening.”
lessons.topic: {{で|de}} “at, in” (where something is done); {{と|to}} “with”; {{から|kara}} and {{まで|made}}

goal.t: 毎晩、家で日本語を勉強します。
goal.r: Maiban, ie de Nihongo o benkyō shimasu.
goal.tr: Every evening I study Japanese at home.

dialog.t: 毎日、何をしますか。
dialog.r: Mainichi, nani o shimasu ka.
dialog.tr: What do you do every day?

dialog.t: 九時から五時まで会社で働きます。
dialog.r: Ku-ji kara go-ji made kaisha de hatarakimasu.
dialog.tr: I work at the office from nine to five.

dialog.t: 晩ご飯は？
dialog.r: Bangohan wa?
dialog.tr: What about dinner?

dialog.t: たいてい友達とレストランで食べます。
dialog.r: Taitei tomodachi to resutoran de tabemasu.
dialog.tr: I usually eat at a restaurant with friends.

dialog.t: 週末は？
dialog.r: Shūmatsu wa?
dialog.tr: And at the weekend?

dialog.t: 週末は家で寝ます！
dialog.r: Shūmatsu wa ie de nemasu!
dialog.tr: At the weekend I sleep at home!

blocks.p: **Where you do something: {{で|de}}.** The place where an action happens takes {{で|de}}: {{家で勉強します|ie de benkyō shimasu}} “I study at home”, {{会社で働きます|kaisha de hatarakimasu}} “I work at the office”. Don't mix it up with {{へ|e}} / {{に|ni}}, which mark where you go **to**. {{で|de}} is where you **are** while you do it.

table: {{図書館へ行きます|toshokan e ikimasu}} I go to the library
{{図書館で勉強します|toshokan de benkyō shimasu}} I study at the library

blocks.p: **Who with: {{と|to}}.** {{友達と|tomodachi to}} “with a friend”, {{家族と|kazoku to}} “with my family”: the same {{と|to}} that means “and” between nouns. On your own is {{一人で|hitori de}}.

**From… to…: {{から|kara}} and {{まで|made}}.** For times and places: {{九時から五時まで|ku-ji kara go-ji made}} “from nine to five”, {{東京から大阪まで|Tōkyō kara Ōsaka made}} “from Tokyo to Osaka”. Each one also works alone: {{月曜日から|getsuyōbi kara}} “from Monday”.
**What do you do?** {{何をしますか。|Nani o shimasu ka.}} Before {{を|o}}, {{何|nan}} is said “nani”.

ex.t: 図書館で本を読みます。
ex.r: Toshokan de hon o yomimasu.
ex.tr: I read books at the library.

ex.t: 友達とカフェで話します。
ex.r: Tomodachi to kafe de hanashimasu.
ex.tr: I talk with friends at a café.

ex.t: 九時から五時まで働きます。
ex.r: Ku-ji kara go-ji made hatarakimasu.
ex.tr: I work from nine to five.

ex.t: 一人で映画を見ます。
ex.r: Hitori de eiga o mimasu.
ex.tr: I watch movies on my own.

ex.t: 週末、何をしますか。
ex.r: Shūmatsu, nani o shimasu ka.
ex.tr: What do you do at the weekend?

ex.t: 駅から家まで歩きます。
ex.r: Eki kara ie made arukimasu.
ex.tr: I walk from the station to my house.

blocks.tip: {{～は？|… wa?}} on its own, with your voice going up, means “what about…?”: {{晩ご飯は？|Bangohan wa?}} “What about dinner?”. A very handy way to keep a conversation going.

mistakes.why: Where you do something takes {{で|de}}. {{に|ni}} is for where you go.
“With” a person is {{と|to}}. {{で|de}} is for places and for means, like {{バスで|basu de}}.

lessons.title: Say what you did yesterday
lessons.summary: Talk about the past: what you did, where you went, and what you didn't do: “I saw a movie with a friend yesterday.”
lessons.topic: {{ました|mashita}} and {{ませんでした|masen deshita}}; {{何も|nani mo}} and {{どこへも|doko e mo}} with a negative

goal.t: 昨日、友達と映画を見ました。
goal.r: Kinō, tomodachi to eiga o mimashita.
goal.tr: I saw a movie with a friend yesterday.

dialog.t: 週末、何をしましたか。
dialog.r: Shūmatsu, nani o shimashita ka.
dialog.tr: What did you do at the weekend?

dialog.t: 土曜日に友達と鎌倉へ行きました。
dialog.r: Doyōbi ni tomodachi to Kamakura e ikimashita.
dialog.tr: On Saturday I went to Kamakura with a friend.

dialog.t: いいですね。日曜日は？
dialog.r: Ii desu ne. Nichiyōbi wa?
dialog.tr: Nice. And on Sunday?

dialog.t: 日曜日はどこへも行きませんでした。家で寝ました。
dialog.r: Nichiyōbi wa doko e mo ikimasen deshita. Ie de nemashita.
dialog.tr: On Sunday I didn't go anywhere. I slept at home.

blocks.means: the form of a verb that shows when something happens: now, in the past, in the future.

blocks.p: **The past: {{ました|mashita}}.** Change {{ます|masu}} to {{ました|mashita}}: {{見ます|mimasu}} → {{見ました|mimashita}} “saw, watched”, {{行きます|ikimasu}} → {{行きました|ikimashita}} “went”. Every verb, no exceptions, the same for everyone.

table: {{見ませんでした|mimasen deshita}} I didn't watch

blocks.p: **Didn't: {{ませんでした|masen deshita}}.** The negative {{ません|masen}}, then {{でした|deshita}}: {{食べませんでした|tabemasen deshita}} “I didn't eat”.

**Nothing, nowhere, nobody.** A question word + {{も|mo}}, with a negative verb: {{何も食べませんでした|nani mo tabemasen deshita}} “I didn't eat anything”, {{どこへも行きませんでした|doko e mo ikimasen deshita}} “I didn't go anywhere”, {{だれも来ませんでした|dare mo kimasen deshita}} “Nobody came”. {{も|mo}} takes the place of {{を|o}}, but comes after {{へ|e}}.

ex.t: 先週、京都へ行きました。
ex.r: Senshū, Kyōto e ikimashita.
ex.tr: I went to Kyoto last week.

ex.t: 今朝は何も食べませんでした。
ex.r: Kesa wa nani mo tabemasen deshita.
ex.tr: I didn't eat anything this morning.

ex.t: 昨日の晩、どこへ行きましたか。
ex.r: Kinō no ban, doko e ikimashita ka.
ex.tr: Where did you go last night?

ex.t: 何時に寝ましたか。
ex.r: Nan-ji ni nemashita ka.
ex.tr: What time did you go to bed?

ex.t: パーティーにだれも来ませんでした。
ex.r: Pātī ni dare mo kimasen deshita.
ex.tr: Nobody came to the party.

ex.t: 去年、日本語の勉強を始めました。
ex.r: Kyonen, Nihongo no benkyō o hajimemashita.
ex.tr: I started studying Japanese last year.

blocks.tip: Past time words: {{昨日|kinō}} yesterday, {{今朝|kesa}} this morning, {{先週|senshū}} last week, {{去年|kyonen}} last year. Like {{明日|ashita}}, they take no {{に|ni}}.

mistakes.why: Japanese shows the past on the verb: {{ました|mashita}}. {{昨日|kinō}} alone isn't enough.

mistakes.wrong: 何を食べませんでした。
mistakes.right: 何も食べませんでした。
mistakes.why: “Nothing” is {{何も|nani mo}} with a negative verb. {{何を|nani o}} asks a question: {{何を食べましたか|nani o tabemashita ka}} “What did you eat?”

practice.q: Choose the missing ending.
practice.t: 先週、京都へ行き___。
practice.tr: I went to Kyoto last week.
practice.why: Last week is the past: {{行きました|ikimashita}}.

practice.q: How do you say “I didn't eat anything”?
options: {{何も食べませんでした。|Nani mo tabemasen deshita.}}
{{何を食べませんでした。|Nani o tabemasen deshita.}}

lessons.title: Invite someone and make plans together
lessons.summary: Invite a friend, say yes, decide when and where, and turn an invitation down politely: “Would you like to have lunch together?”
lessons.topic: {{ませんか|masen ka}} “would you like to…?”; {{ましょう|mashō}} “let's”; {{ましょうか|mashō ka}} “shall we…?”

goal.t: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
goal.r: Issho ni hirugohan o tabemasen ka.
goal.tr: Would you like to have lunch together?

dialog.t: ゆいさん、土曜日に一緒に映画を見ませんか。
dialog.r: Yui-san, doyōbi ni issho ni eiga o mimasen ka.
dialog.tr: Yui, would you like to see a movie together on Saturday?

dialog.t: いいですね。見ましょう。
dialog.r: Ii desu ne. Mimashō.
dialog.tr: Sounds good. Let's!

dialog.t: 何時に会いましょうか。
dialog.r: Nan-ji ni aimashō ka.
dialog.tr: What time shall we meet?

dialog.t: 二時はどうですか。
dialog.r: Ni-ji wa dō desu ka.
dialog.tr: How about two o'clock?

dialog.t: いいですよ。じゃ、二時に駅で会いましょう。
dialog.r: Ii desu yo. Ja, ni-ji ni eki de aimashō.
dialog.tr: Fine. So let's meet at the station at two.

blocks.p: **Inviting: {{～ませんか|… masen ka}}.** Word for word “won't you…?”, a negative question: {{一緒に映画を見ませんか。|Issho ni eiga o mimasen ka.}} “Won't you see a movie with me?”, meaning “Would you like to…?”. It's the most polite way to invite, because it leaves the other person room to say no. {{一緒に|issho ni}} is “together”.
**Let's: {{～ましょう|… mashō}}.** {{見ましょう|mimashō}} “let's watch”, {{行きましょう|ikimashō}} “let's go”. Use it to accept an invitation, or to suggest something you both already want.

**Shall we…? Shall I…?: {{～ましょうか|… mashō ka}}.** To decide something together: {{何時に会いましょうか|nan-ji ni aimashō ka}} “What time shall we meet?”. And to offer help: {{手伝いましょうか|tetsudaimashō ka}} “Shall I help?”.

table: shall we go? shall I go?

blocks.p: **Saying no, nicely.** Japanese rarely says a flat “no” to an invitation. Say {{すみません|sumimasen}} “sorry”, the day, then {{ちょっと…|chotto…}} “it's a bit…”, and let the sentence trail off: {{土曜日はちょっと…|doyōbi wa chotto…}} “Saturday is a bit…”. Everyone understands.

ex.t: コーヒーを飲みませんか。
ex.r: Kōhī o nomimasen ka.
ex.tr: Would you like a coffee?

ex.t: いいですね。行きましょう。
ex.r: Ii desu ne. Ikimashō.
ex.tr: Sounds good. Let's go.

ex.t: どこで会いましょうか。
ex.r: Doko de aimashō ka.
ex.tr: Where shall we meet?

ex.t: 窓を開けましょうか。
ex.r: Mado o akemashō ka.
ex.tr: Shall I open the window?

ex.t: すみません、明日はちょっと…。
ex.r: Sumimasen, ashita wa chotto…
ex.tr: Sorry, tomorrow's a bit… (difficult).

ex.t: じゃ、また今度行きましょう。
ex.r: Ja, mata kondo ikimashō.
ex.tr: Then let's go another time.

blocks.tip: {{いいですね|ii desu ne}} “that sounds good” is the warmest way to say yes. {{ね|ne}} at the end asks the other person to agree with you: “isn't it?”.

mistakes.right: いいですね。見ましょう。
mistakes.why: {{見ませんか|mimasen ka}} is an invitation, not a real negative question. Say yes with {{いいですね|ii desu ne}} or {{～ましょう|… mashō}}: {{はい、見ません|hai, mimasen}} would mean “Yes, I won't watch it”.

mistakes.wrong: 一緒に映画を見ますか。
mistakes.right: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。
mistakes.rw: Issho ni eiga o mimasu ka.
mistakes.rr: Issho ni eiga o mimasen ka.
mistakes.tr: Would you like to see a movie together?
mistakes.why: {{見ますか|mimasu ka}} only asks for information (“Are you going to see a movie?”). To invite, use {{ませんか|masen ka}}.

lessons.title: Describe people, places and things
lessons.summary: Say what things are like, and what they aren't: “The ramen at this shop is really delicious.”
lessons.topic: {{い|i}}-adjectives and {{な|na}}-adjectives; their negatives; {{とても|totemo}} and {{あまり|amari}}

goal.t: この店のラーメンはとてもおいしいです。
goal.r: Kono mise no rāmen wa totemo oishii desu.
goal.tr: The ramen at this shop is really delicious.

dialog.t: 大阪はどうですか。
dialog.r: Ōsaka wa dō desu ka.
dialog.tr: How do you like Osaka?

dialog.t: とてもにぎやかです。食べ物もおいしいです。
dialog.r: Totemo nigiyaka desu. Tabemono mo oishii desu.
dialog.tr: It's very lively. And the food is good.

dialog.t: 家賃は高いですか。
dialog.r: Yachin wa takai desu ka.
dialog.tr: Is the rent expensive?

dialog.t: いいえ、あまり高くないです。でも、私のアパートは静かじゃありません。
dialog.r: Iie, amari takakunai desu. Demo, watashi no apāto wa shizuka ja arimasen.
dialog.tr: No, not very. But my apartment isn't quiet.

blocks.means: a word that describes a person or a thing: big, quiet, delicious.

blocks.p: **Two families of adjectives.** **い-adjectives** end in {{い|i}}: {{高い|takai}} “expensive, tall”, {{おいしい|oishii}} “delicious”, {{大きい|ōkii}} “big”. **な-adjectives** take {{な|na}} before a noun: {{静か|shizuka}} “quiet”, {{にぎやか|nigiyaka}} “lively”, {{元気|genki}} “well, full of energy”. Each family changes in its own way, so learn which family a new adjective is in. (Careful: {{きれい|kirei}} “pretty, clean” is a な-adjective, even though it ends in い.)

**With {{です|desu}}**, both families simply come before it: {{このかばんは高いです|kono kaban wa takai desu}} “This bag is expensive”, {{この町は静かです|kono machi wa shizuka desu}} “This town is quiet”. **Before a noun**, an い-adjective comes as it is, and a な-adjective adds {{な|na}}: {{高いかばん|takai kaban}} “an expensive bag”, {{静かな町|shizuka na machi}} “a quiet town”.

table: {{静かじゃありません|shizuka ja arimasen}}

blocks.p: **Not.** An い-adjective turns its last {{い|i}} into {{くない|kunai}}: {{高い|takai}} → {{高くないです|takakunai desu}} “it isn't expensive” ({{高くありません|takaku arimasen}} means the same, a little more formal). A な-adjective says “not” like a noun: {{静かじゃありません|shizuka ja arimasen}}. One adjective is irregular: {{いい|ii}} “good” → {{よくないです|yokunai desu}}.

**Very, not very.** {{とても|totemo}} is “very”. {{あまり|amari}} “not very” only works with a negative: {{あまり高くないです|amari takakunai desu}} “It isn't very expensive”. To ask what something is like: {{どうですか|dō desu ka}} “How is it?”.

ex.t: 東京は大きい町です。
ex.r: Tōkyō wa ōkii machi desu.
ex.tr: Tokyo is a big city.

ex.t: 京都はきれいな町です。
ex.r: Kyōto wa kirei na machi desu.
ex.tr: Kyoto is a beautiful city.

ex.t: このかばんはあまり高くないです。
ex.r: Kono kaban wa amari takakunai desu.
ex.tr: This bag isn't very expensive.

ex.t: 私の部屋は静かじゃありません。
ex.r: Watashi no heya wa shizuka ja arimasen.
ex.tr: My room isn't quiet.

ex.t: 田中さんはやさしい人です。
ex.r: Tanaka-san wa yasashii hito desu.
ex.tr: Mr Tanaka is a kind person.

ex.t: このパソコンはあまりよくないです。
ex.r: Kono pasokon wa amari yokunai desu.
ex.tr: This computer isn't very good.
ex.note: {{いい|ii}} → {{よくない|yokunai}}

blocks.tip: Japanese often leaves out what it's talking about: {{おいしいです|oishii desu}} alone means “(It's) delicious”. And at the table, plain {{おいしい！|oishii!}} is what everyone says.

mistakes.right: 静かなレストランです。
mistakes.why: A な-adjective needs {{な|na}} before a noun: {{静かなレストラン|shizuka na resutoran}}.
An い-adjective makes its own negative: {{い|i}} → {{くない|kunai}}. {{じゃありません|ja arimasen}} is for nouns and な-adjectives.
{{あまり|amari}} “not very” always goes with a negative.

practice.tr: Kyoto is a beautiful city.
practice.why: {{きれい|kirei}} is a な-adjective: {{きれいな町|kirei na machi}}.

いいえ、あまり広いです。

lessons.title: Say how something was
lessons.summary: Talk about how your trip, the food or the weather was: “The trip was really fun.”
lessons.topic: adjectives in the past: {{かったです|katta desu}} and {{でした|deshita}}; nouns in the past

goal.t: 旅行はとても楽しかったです。
goal.r: Ryokō wa totemo tanoshikatta desu.
goal.tr: The trip was really fun.

dialog.t: 京都はどうでしたか。
dialog.r: Kyōto wa dō deshita ka.
dialog.tr: How was Kyoto?

dialog.t: とてもきれいでした。天気もよかったです。
dialog.r: Totemo kirei deshita. Tenki mo yokatta desu.
dialog.tr: It was really beautiful. And the weather was good.

dialog.t: 寒かったですか。
dialog.r: Samukatta desu ka.
dialog.tr: Was it cold?

dialog.t: いいえ、あまり寒くなかったです。でも、ホテルは高かったです。
dialog.r: Iie, amari samukunakatta desu. Demo, hoteru wa takakatta desu.
dialog.tr: No, not very. But the hotel was expensive.

blocks.p: **い-adjectives: {{い|i}} → {{かった|katta}}.** {{楽しい|tanoshii}} → {{楽しかったです|tanoshikatta desu}} “it was fun”, {{高い|takai}} → {{高かったです|takakatta desu}} “it was expensive”. The negative changes the same way: {{くない|kunai}} → {{くなかった|kunakatta}}, so {{高くなかったです|takakunakatta desu}} “it wasn't expensive”. The past is in the adjective itself; {{です|desu}} stays as it is.

**な-adjectives and nouns: {{でした|deshita}}.** {{です|desu}} becomes {{でした|deshita}}: {{きれいでした|kirei deshita}} “it was beautiful”, {{雨でした|ame deshita}} “it was rainy” (word for word “it was rain”). The negative: {{じゃありませんでした|ja arimasen deshita}}.

table: {{きれいじゃありませんでした|kirei ja arimasen deshita}}

blocks.p: {{いい|ii}} “good” uses {{よ|yo}} again: {{よかったです|yokatta desu}} “it was good”, {{よくなかったです|yokunakatta desu}} “it wasn't good”. {{よかったです|yokatta desu}} also means “I'm glad”. To ask, {{どうでしたか|dō deshita ka}} “How was it?”.

ex.t: 昨日は寒かったです。
ex.r: Kinō wa samukatta desu.
ex.tr: It was cold yesterday.

ex.t: 映画はあまりおもしろくなかったです。
ex.r: Eiga wa amari omoshirokunakatta desu.
ex.tr: The movie wasn't very interesting.

ex.t: ホテルはとてもきれいでした。
ex.r: Hoteru wa totemo kirei deshita.
ex.tr: The hotel was very clean.

ex.t: 昨日は雨でした。
ex.r: Kinō wa ame deshita.
ex.tr: It rained yesterday.
ex.note: word for word “yesterday was rain”: a noun in the past

ex.t: 先週は休みでした。
ex.r: Senshū wa yasumi deshita.
ex.tr: I was off last week.

ex.t: テストはよかったです。
ex.r: Tesuto wa yokatta desu.
ex.tr: The test went well.

blocks.tip: When a friend tells you good news, {{よかったですね！|yokatta desu ne!}} means “I'm so glad for you!”.

mistakes.why: An い-adjective makes its own past: {{い|i}} → {{かった|katta}}, then {{です|desu}}. {{でした|deshita}} is for nouns and な-adjectives.
{{きれい|kirei}} is a な-adjective (even though it ends in い), so its past is {{きれいでした|kirei deshita}}.
{{いい|ii}} changes to {{よ|yo}}: {{よかったです|yokatta desu}}.

practice.t: 旅行は楽し___です。
practice.tr: The trip was fun.

lessons.title: Say what is where
lessons.summary: Say what there is in a place, and where things and people are: “There's a convenience store in front of the station.”
lessons.topic: {{あります|arimasu}} and {{います|imasu}}; {{に|ni}} for where something is; {{が|ga}} for something new

goal.t: 駅の前にコンビニがあります。
goal.r: Eki no mae ni konbini ga arimasu.
goal.tr: There's a convenience store in front of the station.

dialog.t: すみません、この近くに銀行がありますか。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, kono chikaku ni ginkō ga arimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a bank near here?

dialog.t: ええ、あそこにスーパーがありますね。銀行はスーパーの隣にあります。
dialog.r: Ē, asoko ni sūpā ga arimasu ne. Ginkō wa sūpā no tonari ni arimasu.
dialog.tr: Yes. You see the supermarket over there? The bank is next to the supermarket.

dialog.t: ありがとうございます。
dialog.r: Arigatō gozaimasu.
dialog.tr: Thank you.

blocks.p: **Two verbs for being somewhere.** {{あります|arimasu}} for things and places, {{います|imasu}} for people and animals, anything that moves on its own: {{コンビニがあります|konbini ga arimasu}} “there's a convenience store”, {{猫がいます|neko ga imasu}} “there's a cat”.

blocks.means: the person or thing that does the action, or is in the state: **the cat** is sleeping; **a bank** is near here.

blocks.p: **{{が|ga}}: something new.** When you say that something is there, the thing takes {{が|ga}}, not {{は|wa}}: {{駅の前にコンビニがあります|eki no mae ni konbini ga arimasu}} “In front of the station there's a convenience store”. {{が|ga}} marks the subject when it's new information, something you're bringing into the conversation. You'll meet {{が|ga}} again and again.
**Where: {{に|ni}}.** The place where something is takes {{に|ni}}. There are two shapes:

table: {{机の上に本があります。|Tsukue no ue ni hon ga arimasu.}} There's a book on the desk.
{{本は机の上にあります。|Hon wa tsukue no ue ni arimasu.}} The book is on the desk.

blocks.p: The first shape brings in something new ({{が|ga}}). The second talks about something already known ({{は|wa}}) and says where it is. To ask where: {{トイレはどこですか|toire wa doko desu ka}} or {{どこにありますか|doko ni arimasu ka}}.

**Position words** are nouns, joined with {{の|no}}: {{机の上|tsukue no ue}} “on the desk”, word for word “the desk's top”. The main ones: {{上|ue}} on, above; {{下|shita}} under; {{中|naka}} in, inside; {{前|mae}} in front of; {{後ろ|ushiro}} behind; {{隣|tonari}} next to; {{近く|chikaku}} near.

ex.t: 机の上に猫がいます。
ex.r: Tsukue no ue ni neko ga imasu.
ex.tr: There's a cat on the desk.

ex.t: トイレはどこにありますか。

lessons.title: Count people and things
lessons.summary: Say how many people, tickets, bottles or pets: “There are four people in my family.”
lessons.topic: counters: {{人|nin}}, {{枚|mai}}, {{本|hon}}, {{匹|hiki}}, {{つ|tsu}}; {{何人|nan-nin}}, {{いくつ|ikutsu}}

goal.t: 私の家族は四人です。
goal.r: Watashi no kazoku wa yo-nin desu.
goal.tr: There are four people in my family.

dialog.t: いらっしゃいませ。何名様ですか。
dialog.r: Irasshaimase. Nan-mei-sama desu ka.
dialog.tr: Welcome. How many are you?

dialog.t: 三人です。
dialog.r: San-nin desu.
dialog.tr: Three.

dialog.t: こちらへどうぞ。
dialog.r: Kochira e dōzo.
dialog.tr: This way, please.

dialog.t: すみません、ビールを二本と、お皿を三枚ください。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, bīru o ni-hon to, osara o san-mai kudasai.
dialog.tr: Excuse me, two bottles of beer and three plates, please.

dialog.t: かしこまりました。
dialog.r: Kashikomarimashita.
dialog.tr: Certainly.

blocks.means: a word added to a number to say what kind of thing is counted: {{三枚|san-mai}} “three (flat things)”.

blocks.p: **Numbers need counters.** Japanese doesn't put a number straight onto a noun: it adds a **counter**, chosen by the kind of thing. English does this sometimes, in “two **cups** of tea” or “three **sheets** of paper”; Japanese does it every time you count.

table: flat things: tickets, paper, shirts, plates

blocks.p: **Where the number goes.** As with {{つ|tsu}} in the shop, the number and its counter usually come after the particle, just before the verb: {{ビールを二本ください|bīru o ni-hon kudasai}} “two bottles of beer, please”, {{猫が二匹います|neko ga ni-hiki imasu}} “there are two cats”. And {{います|imasu}} also says you have family or pets: {{兄弟が二人います|kyōdai ga futari imasu}} “I have two brothers and sisters”.

Some sounds change: {{本|hon}} and {{匹|hiki}} change with 1, 3, 6, 8 and 10 ({{一本|ippon}}, {{三本|sanbon}}, {{六本|roppon}}). For people, one and two are special words: {{一人|hitori}}, {{二人|futari}}; then {{三人|san-nin}}, {{四人|yo-nin}}, {{五人|go-nin}}.

ex.t: 兄が一人います。
ex.r: Ani ga hitori imasu.
ex.tr: I have one older brother.

ex.t: 切手を三枚ください。
ex.r: Kitte o san-mai kudasai.
ex.tr: Three stamps, please.

ex.t: 猫が二匹います。
ex.r: Neko ga ni-hiki imasu.
ex.tr: I have two cats.

ex.t: ビールを二本お願いします。
ex.r: Bīru o ni-hon onegaishimasu.
ex.tr: Two bottles of beer, please.

ex.t: 学生は何人いますか。
ex.r: Gakusei wa nan-nin imasu ka.
ex.tr: How many students are there?

ex.t: りんごを五つ買いました。
ex.r: Ringo o itsutsu kaimashita.
ex.tr: I bought five apples.

blocks.tip: In restaurants, staff count customers with the polite counter {{名|mei}}: {{何名様ですか|nan-mei-sama desu ka}} “How many are you?”. You answer with {{人|nin}}: {{二人です|futari desu}}.

mistakes.right: ビールを三本ください。
mistakes.why: A number needs its counter, and comes after {{を|o}}: {{ビールを三本|bīru o sanbon}}.
{{人|nin}} counts people only. Small animals: {{匹|hiki}}.

lessons.title: Say what you want and what you'd like to do
lessons.summary: Say what you'd like to have and to do, and go somewhere to do something: “I want to eat sushi in Japan.”
lessons.topic: {{～たいです|… tai desu}}; {{ほしいです|hoshii desu}}; {{～に行きます|… ni ikimasu}} “go to do”

goal.t: 日本でお寿司を食べたいです。
goal.r: Nihon de osushi o tabetai desu.
goal.tr: I want to eat sushi in Japan.

dialog.t: 夏休みに何をしたいですか。
dialog.r: Natsuyasumi ni nani o shitai desu ka.
dialog.tr: What do you want to do in the summer holidays?

dialog.t: 北海道へ行きたいです。おいしい魚を食べたいです。
dialog.r: Hokkaidō e ikitai desu. Oishii sakana o tabetai desu.
dialog.tr: I want to go to Hokkaido. I want to eat good fish.

dialog.t: いいですね。
dialog.r: Ii desu ne.
dialog.tr: Sounds great.

dialog.t: それから、新しいカメラがほしいです。北海道へ写真を撮りに行きます！
dialog.r: Sorekara, atarashii kamera ga hoshii desu. Hokkaidō e shashin o tori ni ikimasu!
dialog.tr: And I want a new camera. I'm going to Hokkaido to take pictures!

blocks.means: the part of a verb that stays when its ending changes: {{食べ|tabe}} in {{食べます|tabemasu}} and {{食べたい|tabetai}}.

blocks.p: **Want to do: stem + {{たい|tai}}.** Take the {{ます|masu}} form, drop {{ます|masu}}, and add {{たいです|tai desu}}: {{食べます|tabemasu}} → {{食べたいです|tabetai desu}} “I want to eat”, {{行きます|ikimasu}} → {{行きたいです|ikitai desu}} “I want to go”.
{{たい|tai}} turns the verb into an い-adjective, so it changes exactly like {{高い|takai}}: {{行きたくないです|ikitakunai desu}} “I don't want to go”, {{行きたかったです|ikitakatta desu}} “I wanted to go”.
**Want a thing: {{ほしい|hoshii}}.** {{ほしい|hoshii}} is an い-adjective, and what you want takes {{が|ga}}: {{新しいカメラがほしいです|atarashii kamera ga hoshii desu}} “I want a new camera”.

**Go somewhere to do something: stem + {{に行きます|ni ikimasu}}.** {{写真を撮りに行きます|shashin o tori ni ikimasu}} “I'm going (there) to take pictures”, {{昼ご飯を食べに行きませんか|hirugohan o tabe ni ikimasen ka}} “Shall we go and have lunch?”. It works with {{来ます|kimasu}} and {{帰ります|kaerimasu}} too.

ex.t: 今日は何もしたくないです。
ex.r: Kyō wa nani mo shitakunai desu.
ex.tr: I don't want to do anything today.

ex.t: 新しいスマホがほしいです。
ex.r: Atarashii sumaho ga hoshii desu.
ex.tr: I want a new smartphone.

ex.t: 昨日は映画を見たかったです。
ex.r: Kinō wa eiga o mitakatta desu.
ex.tr: I wanted to see a movie yesterday.

ex.t: 週末、海へ泳ぎに行きます。
ex.r: Shūmatsu, umi e oyogi ni ikimasu.
ex.tr: At the weekend I'm going to the sea to swim.

ex.t: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べに行きませんか。
ex.r: Issho ni hirugohan o tabe ni ikimasen ka.
ex.tr: Shall we go and have lunch together?

ex.t: 何が飲みたいですか。
ex.r: Nani ga nomitai desu ka.
ex.tr: What would you like to drink?
ex.note: with {{たい|tai}}, the object can take {{を|o}} or {{が|ga}}

blocks.tip: Asking a teacher or a customer {{飲みたいですか|nomitai desu ka}} “do you want to drink?” sounds a little too direct. Offer with {{～ませんか|… masen ka}} instead: {{コーヒーを飲みませんか|kōhī o nomimasen ka}}.

mistakes.wrong: 日本へ行きますたいです。
mistakes.tr: I want to go to Japan.
mistakes.why: {{たい|tai}} goes on the stem: drop {{ます|masu}} first. {{行きます|ikimasu}} → {{行きたいです|ikitai desu}}.

mistakes.wrong: 行きたいじゃありません。
mistakes.why: {{たい|tai}} works like an い-adjective: {{たい|tai}} → {{たくない|takunai}}.

practice.q: Choose the missing ending.
practice.t: 北海道へ行き___です。
practice.tr: I want to go to Hokkaido.
practice.why: Stem + {{たい|tai}}: {{行きたいです|ikitai desu}}.

{{行きませんたいです。|Ikimasen tai desu.}}

practice.q: Choose the missing word.
practice.t: 新しいかばん___ほしいです。

practice.why: What you want takes {{が|ga}} with {{ほしい|hoshii}}.

lines.r: Onaka ga sukimashita ne. Nani o tabetai desu ka.
lines.tr: I'm hungry, aren't you? What do you want to eat?

options: ラーメンを食べたいです。

options: じゃ、食べに行きましょう。
じゃ、食べたいに行きましょう。
lines.why: Going to do something: stem + {{に|ni}}: {{食べに行きましょう|tabe ni ikimashō}}.

answers.r: Kotoshi wa Nihon e ikitai desu. Atarashii jitensha mo hoshii desu.

lessons.title: Say what you like and what you're good at
lessons.summary: Talk about likes and dislikes, what you're good and bad at, and what you understand: “I like Japanese movies.”
lessons.topic: {{好き|suki}}, {{嫌い|kirai}}, {{上手|jōzu}}, {{下手|heta}} with {{が|ga}}; {{わかります|wakarimasu}}; {{どんな|donna}}

goal.t: 私は日本の映画が好きです。
goal.r: Watashi wa Nihon no eiga ga suki desu.
goal.tr: I like Japanese movies.

dialog.t: トムさんはどんな音楽が好きですか。
dialog.r: Tomu-san wa donna ongaku ga suki desu ka.
dialog.tr: Tom, what kind of music do you like?

dialog.t: ジャズが大好きです。ゆいさんは？
dialog.r: Jazu ga daisuki desu. Yui-san wa?
dialog.tr: I love jazz. What about you?

dialog.t: 私はカラオケが好きです。でも、歌は下手です。
dialog.r: Watashi wa karaoke ga suki desu. Demo, uta wa heta desu.
dialog.tr: I like karaoke. But I'm bad at singing.

dialog.t: 私も下手です。でも、カラオケは楽しいですね。
dialog.r: Watashi mo heta desu. Demo, karaoke wa tanoshii desu ne.
dialog.tr: Me too. But karaoke is fun, isn't it?

blocks.p: **{{好きです|suki desu}}: “is liked”.** {{好き|suki}} is a な-adjective, not a verb. So Japanese says, word for word, “As for me, Japanese movies are liked”: {{私は日本の映画が好きです|watashi wa Nihon no eiga ga suki desu}}. The person who likes takes {{は|wa}}; **what you like takes {{が|ga}}**, never {{を|o}}.

table: strong: {{あまり好きじゃありません|amari suki ja arimasen}} is softer

blocks.p: **The same {{が|ga}}** goes with {{上手|jōzu}} “good at”, {{下手|heta}} “bad at”, and the verb {{わかります|wakarimasu}} “understand”: {{日本語がわかります|Nihongo ga wakarimasu}} “I understand Japanese”. To ask “what kind of”, use {{どんな|donna}} before the noun: {{どんな料理が好きですか|donna ryōri ga suki desu ka}} “What kind of food do you like?”.
Before a noun, {{好き|suki}} takes {{な|na}}, like any な-adjective: {{好きな食べ物|suki na tabemono}} “favourite food”. {{好きな食べ物は何ですか。|Suki na tabemono wa nan desu ka.}} “What's your favourite food?”

ex.t: 猫が大好きです。
ex.r: Neko ga daisuki desu.
ex.tr: I love cats.

ex.t: 私は野菜があまり好きじゃありません。
ex.r: Watashi wa yasai ga amari suki ja arimasen.
ex.tr: I don't really like vegetables.

ex.t: 田中さんは料理が上手です。
ex.r: Tanaka-san wa ryōri ga jōzu desu.
ex.tr: Mr Tanaka is a good cook.

ex.t: 私は歌が下手です。
ex.r: Watashi wa uta ga heta desu.
ex.tr: I'm bad at singing.

ex.t: 日本語が少しわかります。
ex.r: Nihongo ga sukoshi wakarimasu.
ex.tr: I understand a little Japanese.

ex.t: 好きな食べ物は何ですか。
ex.r: Suki na tabemono wa nan desu ka.
ex.tr: What's your favourite food?

blocks.tip: Don't call yourself {{上手|jōzu}}: it sounds like boasting. When someone praises your Japanese, {{日本語が上手ですね！|Nihongo ga jōzu desu ne!}}, the modest answer is {{いいえ、まだまだです|iie, madamada desu}} “No, I've still got a long way to go”.

mistakes.rw: Watashi wa neko o suki desu.
mistakes.rr: Watashi wa neko ga suki desu.
mistakes.why: {{好き|suki}} is an adjective, not a verb: what you like takes {{が|ga}}.
{{わかります|wakarimasu}} takes {{が|ga}}, like {{好き|suki}}.

lessons.summary: Ask and answer “who?” and “which?”, and set two things side by side: “I eat fish, but I don't eat meat.”
lessons.topic: question word + {{が|ga}}; answering with {{が|ga}}; {{は|wa}} for contrast; {{が|ga}} “but”

goal.t: 魚は食べますが、肉は食べません。

dialog.t: ありがとうございます。料理は好きですが、掃除は嫌いです。
dialog.r: Arigatō gozaimasu. Ryōri wa suki desu ga, sōji wa kirai desu.
dialog.tr: Thank you. I like cooking, but I hate cleaning.

blocks.p: **Who? Which? Always {{が|ga}}.** A question word that is the subject takes {{が|ga}}, never {{は|wa}}: {{だれが作りましたか|dare ga tsukurimashita ka}} “Who made it?”, {{どれがいいですか|dore ga ii desu ka}} “Which one is good?”. The answer takes {{が|ga}} too: {{私が作りました|watashi ga tsukurimashita}} “I made it”, meaning “it was me”.

Why? {{は|wa}} marks what you're already talking about, and then says something new about it. {{が|ga}} puts the spotlight on the subject itself: the subject **is** the news. A question word is always the news, and so is its answer.

table: the topic: “as for…”, then the news
{{田中さんは来ました。|Tanaka-san wa kimashita.}} Mr Tanaka? He came.
{{田中さんが来ました。|Tanaka-san ga kimashita.}} Mr Tanaka came (it was him).
{{だれが来ましたか。|Dare ga kimashita ka.}} Who came?

blocks.p: **{{は|wa}} for contrast.** {{は|wa}} can also set two things against each other: {{魚は食べますが、肉は食べません|sakana wa tabemasu ga, niku wa tabemasen}}, “Fish I eat, but meat I don't”. Here {{は|wa}} even takes the place of {{を|o}}. This is why a negative so often has {{は|wa}}: {{お酒は飲みません|osake wa nomimasen}} hints “alcohol, no (but other things, yes)”.

**{{が|ga}} “but”.** At the end of a sentence, before a comma, {{が|ga}} joins two sentences: {{好きですが、上手じゃありません|suki desu ga, jōzu ja arimasen}} “I like it, but I'm not good at it”. {{でも|demo}} “but” at the start of the next sentence does the same.

ex.r: Dare ga kimashita ka.
ex.tr: Who came?

ex.t: 田中さんが来ました。

blocks.tip: If you're unsure, ask yourself: is this word the new information, the answer to “who?” or “what?” (→ {{が|ga}}), or is it what we're talking about (→ {{は|wa}})?

As the answer to “Who made it?”, the person is the news: {{が|ga}}. {{私は作りました|watashi wa tsukurimashita}} sounds like “As for me, I made (something)”.

blocks.means: the form of a verb ending in {{て|te}} or {{で|de}} ({{食べて|tabete}}, {{読んで|yonde}}), used to ask, to link actions and much more.

blocks.p: **The て-form.** Every verb has a form ending in {{て|te}} or {{で|de}}. Alone it doesn't mean much, but a whole set of useful patterns is built on it, starting with this one: て-form + {{ください|kudasai}} “please do…”.

blocks.means: one of the three families of Japanese verbs; each family makes its forms in its own way.

blocks.p: **Making it from the {{ます|masu}} form.** It depends on the verb's group. **Group 3** has just two verbs: {{します|shimasu}} → {{して|shite}}, {{来ます|kimasu}} → {{来て|kite}}. **Group 2**: drop {{ます|masu}} and add {{て|te}}: {{食べます|tabemasu}} → {{食べて|tabete}}, {{見ます|mimasu}} → {{見て|mite}}. Every verb whose stem ends in an e-sound ({{食べ|tabe}}, {{寝|ne}}, {{開け|ake}}) is group 2, and so are a few with an i-sound, like {{見ます|mimasu}}, {{起きます|okimasu}}, {{降ります|orimasu}} and {{います|imasu}}: learn those as you meet them. **Group 1** is all the rest, and the sound before {{ます|masu}} decides the change:

table: {{買います|kaimasu}} → {{買って|katte}}, {{待ちます|machimasu}} → {{待って|matte}}, {{帰ります|kaerimasu}} → {{帰って|kaette}}
{{飲みます|nomimasu}} → {{飲んで|nonde}}, {{遊びます|asobimasu}} → {{遊んで|asonde}}
{{書きます|kakimasu}} → {{書いて|kaite}}; but {{行きます|ikimasu}} → {{行って|itte}}

blocks.p: It looks like a lot, but it's all about sound: the changes make the words easier to say. Learn one example from each row and the rest follow. {{行きます|ikimasu}} is the only exception in group 1.

**Asking: て-form + {{ください|kudasai}}.** {{待ってください|matte kudasai}} “please wait”, {{見てください|mite kudasai}} “please look”. It's polite, but it's still a request that the other person is expected to follow: teachers, staff and doctors use it all the time. When you ask a favour, start with {{すみません|sumimasen}}; later lessons give you softer ways.

ex.tr: Sorry, could you say that again, please?

blocks.tip: {{わかりました|wakarimashita}} “I understand, will do” is the natural answer to a request. Between friends, {{ください|kudasai}} is often dropped: {{ちょっと待って！|chotto matte!}} “Wait a sec!”.

lessons.title: Ask if you may, and say what's not allowed
lessons.summary: Ask permission, give it, and understand the rules: “May I take photos here?” “Not inside, please.”
lessons.topic: {{～てもいいですか|… te mo ii desu ka}}; {{～てはいけません|… te wa ikemasen}}

goal.t: ここで写真を撮ってもいいですか。
goal.r: Koko de shashin o totte mo ii desu ka.
goal.tr: May I take photos here?

dialog.t: すみません、ここで写真を撮ってもいいですか。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, koko de shashin o totte mo ii desu ka.
dialog.tr: Excuse me, may I take photos here?

dialog.r: Soto wa ii desu yo. Demo, naka de shashin o totte wa ikemasen.
dialog.tr: Outside is fine. But you mustn't take photos inside.

blocks.p: **May I…?: て-form + {{もいいですか|mo ii desu ka}}.** Word for word “Even if I do…, is it good?”: {{写真を撮ってもいいですか|shashin o totte mo ii desu ka}} “May I take a photo?”. To say yes: {{はい、どうぞ|hai, dōzo}} “Yes, go ahead” or {{いいですよ|ii desu yo}} “Sure”.

**Not allowed: て-form + {{はいけません|wa ikemasen}}.** {{ここでたばこを吸ってはいけません|koko de tabako o sutte wa ikemasen}} “You mustn't smoke here”. This is strong: the language of rules, signs and parents. To turn down someone's request, people say {{すみません、ちょっと…|sumimasen, chotto…}} instead, just as with invitations.

table: {{入ってもいいですか|haitte mo ii desu ka}}
{{はい、どうぞ|hai, dōzo}} / {{いいですよ|ii desu yo}}
{{入ってはいけません|haitte wa ikemasen}}

lessons.title: Say what's happening now, and how things are
lessons.summary: Say what you're doing right now, and talk about states: where you live, whether you're married, what you know: “I'm making dinner right now.”
lessons.topic: {{～ています|… te imasu}}: something in progress, and a state

goal.t: 今、晩ご飯を作っています。
goal.r: Ima, bangohan o tsukutte imasu.
goal.tr: I'm making dinner right now.

dialog.t: もしもし、ケンさん？今、何をしていますか。
dialog.r: Moshimoshi, Ken-san? Ima, nani o shite imasu ka.
dialog.tr: Hello, Ken? What are you doing right now?

dialog.t: テレビでサッカーを見ています。
dialog.r: Terebi de sakkā o mite imasu.
dialog.tr: I'm watching football on TV.

dialog.t: そうですか。マリアさんの電話番号を知っていますか。
dialog.r: Sō desu ka. Maria-san no denwa bangō o shitte imasu ka.
dialog.tr: I see. Do you know Maria's phone number?

dialog.t: すみません、知りません。でも、ジョンさんが知っていますよ。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, shirimasen. Demo, Jon-san ga shitte imasu yo.
dialog.tr: Sorry, I don't. But John knows it.

blocks.p: **Doing it right now: て-form + {{います|imasu}}.** {{作っています|tsukutte imasu}} “I'm making”, {{見ています|mite imasu}} “I'm watching”. This {{います|imasu}} is the verb “to be (somewhere)”: you **are** in the middle of doing it. It changes like any {{ます|masu}} verb: {{見ていません|mite imasen}} “I'm not watching”, {{見ていました|mite imashita}} “I was watching”.

**Being in a state.** With some verbs, {{ています|te imasu}} describes a state that began earlier and is still true: {{住んでいます|sunde imasu}} “I live (there)”, word for word “I've settled there”; {{結婚しています|kekkon shite imasu}} “I'm married”; {{知っています|shitte imasu}} “I know”; {{働いています|hataraite imasu}} “I work (at…)”; {{持っています|motte imasu}} “I have, I own”. English uses the simple present for these; Japanese needs {{ています|te imasu}}.

table: {{今、雨が降っています。|Ima, ame ga futte imasu.}}
{{東京に住んでいます。|Tōkyō ni sunde imasu.}}
{{田中さんを知っています。|Tanaka-san o shitte imasu.}}

blocks.p: **One odd one out:** “I don't know” is {{知りません|shirimasen}}, not {{知っていません|shitte imasen}}.

ex.t: 子供たちは公園で遊んでいます。
ex.r: Kodomotachi wa kōen de asonde imasu.
ex.tr: The children are playing in the park.

ex.t: 私は大阪に住んでいます。
ex.r: Watashi wa Ōsaka ni sunde imasu.
ex.tr: I live in Osaka.

ex.t: 姉は銀行で働いています。
ex.r: Ane wa ginkō de hataraite imasu.
ex.tr: My older sister works at a bank.

ex.t: 田中さんは結婚しています。
ex.r: Tanaka-san wa kekkon shite imasu.
ex.tr: Mr Tanaka is married.

ex.t: 車を持っていますか。
ex.r: Kuruma o motte imasu ka.
ex.tr: Do you have a car?

ex.t: すみません、知りません。
ex.r: Sumimasen, shirimasen.
ex.tr: Sorry, I don't know.

blocks.tip: {{もしもし|moshimoshi}} is “hello” on the phone only.

“I don't know” is simply {{知りません|shirimasen}}.

lessons.title: Tell what you do, step by step
lessons.summary: Link actions in order, and join descriptions together: “In the morning I get up, have a shower and go to work.”
lessons.topic: {{～て、～て|… te, … te}}; {{～てから|… te kara}}; adjectives joined with {{くて|kute}} and {{で|de}}

goal.t: 朝起きて、シャワーを浴びて、会社へ行きます。
goal.r: Asa okite, shawā o abite, kaisha e ikimasu.
goal.tr: In the morning I get up, have a shower and go to work.

dialog.t: 昨日は何をしましたか。
dialog.r: Kinō wa nani o shimashita ka.
dialog.tr: What did you do yesterday?

dialog.t: 友達と新宿へ行って、買い物をして、映画を見ました。
dialog.r: Tomodachi to Shinjuku e itte, kaimono o shite, eiga o mimashita.
dialog.tr: I went to Shinjuku with a friend, did some shopping and saw a movie.

dialog.t: どうでしたか。
dialog.r: Dō deshita ka.
dialog.tr: How was it?

dialog.t: 映画は長くて、ちょっと退屈でした。でも、レストランは安くておいしかったです。
dialog.r: Eiga wa nagakute, chotto taikutsu deshita. Demo, resutoran wa yasukute oishikatta desu.
dialog.tr: The movie was long and a bit boring. But the restaurant was cheap and good.

blocks.p: **And then… and then…: the て-form.** To tell several actions in a row, put every verb except the last in the て-form. Only the last verb shows when it happens and how polite you are: {{起きて、シャワーを浴びて、会社へ行きます|okite, shawā o abite, kaisha e ikimasu}} “I get up, shower and go to work” (every day); {{…会社へ行きました|… kaisha e ikimashita}} “…and went to work” (yesterday).
**After doing…: て-form + {{から|kara}}.** {{から|kara}} makes the order clear: {{宿題をしてから、テレビを見ます|shukudai o shite kara, terebi o mimasu}} “I'll watch TV after I do my homework”.

**Joining descriptions.** An い-adjective changes {{い|i}} to {{くて|kute}}: {{安くておいしい|yasukute oishii}} “cheap and good” ({{いい|ii}} → {{よくて|yokute}}). A な-adjective or a noun adds {{で|de}}: {{静かできれい|shizuka de kirei}} “quiet and pretty”, {{兄は医者で…|ani wa isha de…}} “my brother is a doctor and…”.

table: {{起きて、食べて、出かけます|okite, tabete, dekakemasu}} I get up, eat and go out
{{安くておいしい|yasukute oishii}} cheap and good
{{静かできれい|shizuka de kirei}} quiet and pretty

ex.t: 昨日は図書館へ行って、勉強しました。
ex.r: Kinō wa toshokan e itte, benkyō shimashita.
ex.tr: Yesterday I went to the library and studied.

ex.t: このアパートは広くて、明るいです。
ex.r: Kono apāto wa hirokute, akarui desu.
ex.tr: This apartment is big and bright.

ex.t: 京都は静かで、きれいな町です。
ex.r: Kyōto wa shizuka de, kirei na machi desu.
ex.tr: Kyoto is a quiet, beautiful city.

ex.t: 兄は医者で、東京に住んでいます。
ex.r: Ani wa isha de, Tōkyō ni sunde imasu.

lessons.title: Talk casually with friends
lessons.summary: Switch to the style friends use with each other: “Are you free tomorrow? Want to go and see a movie?”
lessons.topic: plain forms: the dictionary form, the {{ない|nai}} form, {{だ|da}}; questions without {{か|ka}}

goal.t: 明日、一緒に映画を見に行かない？
goal.r: Ashita, issho ni eiga o mi ni ikanai?
goal.tr: Want to go and see a movie together tomorrow?

dialog.t: ケン、明日ひま？
dialog.r: Ken, ashita hima?
dialog.tr: Ken, are you free tomorrow?

dialog.t: うん、ひまだよ。
dialog.r: Un, hima da yo.
dialog.tr: Yeah, I'm free.

dialog.t: 一緒に映画を見に行かない？
dialog.r: Issho ni eiga o mi ni ikanai?
dialog.tr: Want to go and see a movie together?

dialog.t: いいね！何を見る？
dialog.r: Ii ne! Nani o miru?
dialog.tr: Great! What shall we see?

dialog.r: Atarashii anime wa dō?
dialog.tr: How about the new anime?

dialog.t: いいよ。何時に行く？
dialog.r: Ii yo. Nan-ji ni iku?
dialog.tr: Sure. What time shall we go?

blocks.p: **Two styles.** So far everything has been in the polite style, with {{です|desu}} and {{ます|masu}}: right with people you don't know well, at work and in shops. With friends and family, Japanese uses the **plain** style. Polite forms with close friends sound distant; plain forms with your boss sound rude. You need both, and the plain forms are also the building blocks of many patterns in the coming lessons.

blocks.means: the casual form of a verb or adjective, used with friends and inside longer sentences: {{行く|iku}} instead of {{行きます|ikimasu}}.
the plain present of a verb, the form you find in a dictionary: {{食べる|taberu}}, {{行く|iku}}, {{する|suru}}.

blocks.p: **The dictionary form** (plain “do, will do”). Group 2: drop {{ます|masu}}, add {{る|ru}}: {{食べます|tabemasu}} → {{食べる|taberu}}. Group 1: the i-sound before {{ます|masu}} becomes a u-sound: {{行きます|ikimasu}} → {{行く|iku}}, {{飲みます|nomimasu}} → {{飲む|nomu}}, {{待ちます|machimasu}} → {{待つ|matsu}}, {{買います|kaimasu}} → {{買う|kau}}. Group 3: {{する|suru}} and {{来る|kuru}}.

**The ない form** (plain “don't”). Group 2: drop {{ます|masu}}, add {{ない|nai}}: {{食べない|tabenai}}. Group 1: the i-sound becomes an a-sound, then {{ない|nai}}: {{行かない|ikanai}}, {{飲まない|nomanai}}, {{待たない|matanai}}; but a verb in {{います|imasu}} takes {{わ|wa}}: {{買わない|kawanai}}. Group 3: {{しない|shinai}}, {{来ない|konai}}. And {{ある|aru}} “there is” has the plain negative {{ない|nai}}.

**Adjectives and nouns.** い-adjectives just drop {{です|desu}}: {{高い|takai}}, {{高くない|takakunai}}. Nouns and な-adjectives change {{です|desu}} to {{だ|da}}: {{ひまだ|hima da}} “I'm free”, and “not” is {{じゃない|ja nai}}: {{ひまじゃない|hima ja nai}}. In a question, {{だ|da}} disappears: {{ひま？|hima?}} “Are you free?”

**Casual questions** drop {{か|ka}}: just raise your voice. {{行く？|iku?}} “Are you going?”. A negative question invites, like {{ませんか|masen ka}}: {{行かない？|ikanai?}} “Want to go?”. “Yes” and “no” are {{うん|un}} and {{ううん|uun}}, and little words at the end add feeling: {{よ|yo}} “I'm telling you”, {{ね|ne}} “isn't it?”.

ex.t: 明日、何する？
ex.r: Ashita, nani suru?
ex.tr: What are you doing tomorrow?

blocks.tip: In casual speech, particles like {{を|o}} and {{は|wa}} are often dropped: {{映画見る？|eiga miru?}} “Want to watch a movie?”. In this course they mostly stay, so you can see how the sentence is built.

Group 1: the i-sound becomes an a-sound before {{ない|nai}}: {{行かない|ikanai}}.
Verbs in {{います|imasu}} (like {{買います|kaimasu}}) take {{わ|wa}}: {{買わない|kawanai}}.

lessons.title: Chat casually about what happened
lessons.summary: Tell a friend what you did and how it was, in the casual style: “I went to Kyoto yesterday. It was so much fun!”
lessons.topic: the plain past: {{た|ta}} and {{なかった|nakatta}}; {{だった|datta}}; {{かった|katta}}

goal.t: 昨日、京都に行った。すごく楽しかった！
goal.r: Kinō, Kyōto ni itta. Sugoku tanoshikatta!
goal.tr: I went to Kyoto yesterday. It was so much fun!

dialog.t: 週末、何した？
dialog.r: Shūmatsu, nani shita?
dialog.tr: What did you do at the weekend?

dialog.t: 友達と富士山に登った。
dialog.r: Tomodachi to Fujisan ni nobotta.
dialog.tr: I climbed Mt Fuji with some friends.

dialog.t: え、すごい！大変だった？
dialog.r: E, sugoi! Taihen datta?
dialog.tr: Whoa, amazing! Was it hard?

dialog.t: うん、大変だった。でも、景色はすごくきれいだった。
dialog.r: Un, taihen datta. Demo, keshiki wa sugoku kirei datta.
dialog.tr: Yeah, it was hard. But the view was really beautiful.

dialog.t: 写真、撮った？
dialog.r: Shashin, totta?
dialog.tr: Did you take pictures?

dialog.t: ううん、撮らなかった。カメラを忘れた…。
dialog.r: Uun, toranakatta. Kamera o wasureta…
dialog.tr: No, I didn't. I forgot my camera…

blocks.means: the plain past of a verb. It's made like the て-form, with {{た|ta}} or {{だ|da}}: {{食べた|tabeta}}, {{飲んだ|nonda}}.

blocks.p: **The plain past: {{て|te}} becomes {{た|ta}}.** You already know the て-form, and the plain past is the same with {{た|ta}} (or {{だ|da}} where the て-form has {{で|de}}): {{食べて|tabete}} → {{食べた|tabeta}} “ate”, {{行って|itte}} → {{行った|itta}} “went”, {{飲んで|nonde}} → {{飲んだ|nonda}} “drank”, {{して|shite}} → {{した|shita}} “did”.

**Didn't: {{なかった|nakatta}}.** Take the ない form and change {{ない|nai}} to {{なかった|nakatta}}, the way {{高い|takai}} becomes {{高かった|takakatta}}: {{行かなかった|ikanakatta}} “didn't go”, {{食べなかった|tabenakatta}} “didn't eat”.

**Adjectives and nouns.** い-adjectives drop {{です|desu}}: {{楽しかった|tanoshikatta}} “it was fun”. Nouns and な-adjectives take {{だった|datta}}, and “wasn't” is {{じゃなかった|ja nakatta}}: {{大変だった|taihen datta}} “it was hard”, {{雨じゃなかった|ame ja nakatta}} “it didn't rain”.

ex.t: 朝ご飯、食べた？
ex.r: Asagohan, tabeta?
ex.tr: Did you have breakfast?

ex.t: ううん、食べなかった。
ex.r: Uun, tabenakatta.
ex.tr: No, I didn't.

ex.t: 映画はすごくおもしろかった。
ex.r: Eiga wa sugoku omoshirokatta.
ex.tr: The movie was really good.

ex.t: テストは簡単だった。
ex.r: Tesuto wa kantan datta.
ex.tr: The test was easy.

ex.t: 昨日は休みじゃなかった。
ex.r: Kinō wa yasumi ja nakatta.
ex.tr: Yesterday wasn't a day off.

ex.t: 週末はどこにも行かなかった。
ex.r: Shūmatsu wa doko ni mo ikanakatta.
ex.tr: I didn't go anywhere at the weekend.

blocks.tip: {{すごい！|sugoi!}} “amazing!” and {{すごく|sugoku}} “really, so” are everywhere in casual talk: {{すごくおいしかった|sugoku oishikatta}} “it was so good”.

mistakes.why: The plain past follows the て-form: {{行って|itte}} → {{行った|itta}}.
An い-adjective makes its own past: {{楽しかった|tanoshikatta}}. {{だった|datta}} is for nouns and な-adjectives.

lessons.title: Say what you think, and what someone said
lessons.summary: Give your opinion, and pass on what others said: “I think Japanese is interesting.” “Mr Tanaka said there's no problem.”
lessons.topic: plain form + {{と思います|to omoimasu}}; {{～と言っていました|… to itte imashita}}

goal.t: 日本語はおもしろいと思います。
goal.r: Nihongo wa omoshiroi to omoimasu.
goal.tr: I think Japanese is interesting.

dialog.t: この計画はどう思いますか。
dialog.r: Kono keikaku wa dō omoimasu ka.
dialog.tr: What do you think of this plan?

dialog.t: いいと思います。でも、ちょっと高いと思います。
dialog.r: Ii to omoimasu. Demo, chotto takai to omoimasu.
dialog.tr: I think it's good. But I think it's a bit expensive.

dialog.t: そうですね。田中さんは何と言っていましたか。
dialog.r: Sō desu ne. Tanaka-san wa nan to itte imashita ka.
dialog.tr: Hmm, yes. What did Mr Tanaka say?

dialog.t: 問題ないと言っていました。
dialog.r: Mondai nai to itte imashita.
dialog.tr: He said there's no problem.

dialog.t: わかりました。じゃ、やりましょう。
dialog.r: Wakarimashita. Ja, yarimashō.
dialog.tr: All right. Then let's do it.

blocks.p: **I think…: plain form + {{と思います|to omoimasu}}.** What you think comes first, in the plain form, then {{と|to}} (a quotation mark you can hear), then {{思います|omoimasu}} “I think”: {{おもしろいと思います|omoshiroi to omoimasu}} “I think it's interesting”, {{田中さんは来ると思います|Tanaka-san wa kuru to omoimasu}} “I think Mr Tanaka will come”.

Nouns and な-adjectives need {{だ|da}} before {{と|to}}: {{便利だと思います|benri da to omoimasu}} “I think it's convenient”. For “I don't think…”, Japanese usually puts the “not” inside the thought: {{来ないと思います|konai to omoimasu}} “I don't think he'll come”, word for word “I think he won't come”.

table: {{雨が降ると思います。|Ame ga furu to omoimasu.}}
{{便利だと思います。|Benri da to omoimasu.}}
{{いい考えだと思います。|Ii kangae da to omoimasu.}}
I think it's a good idea.
{{来ないと思います。|Konai to omoimasu.}}

blocks.p: **What do you think?: {{どう思いますか|dō omoimasu ka}}.** Answers often begin with {{そうですね…|sō desu ne…}} “Let me see…”.

**Someone said…: plain form + {{と言っていました|to itte imashita}}.** To pass on what someone said: {{田中さんは来ると言っていました|Tanaka-san wa kuru to itte imashita}} “Mr Tanaka said he'd come”. {{と|to}} again marks the words being quoted.

ex.t: 日本の電車は便利だと思います。
ex.r: Nihon no densha wa benri da to omoimasu.
ex.tr: I think Japanese trains are convenient.

ex.t: 明日は雨が降ると思います。
ex.r: Ashita wa ame ga furu to omoimasu.

lessons.title: Say why
lessons.summary: Give reasons and ask why: “I have an early start tomorrow, so I'm going to bed early.”
lessons.topic: {{から|kara}} and {{ので|node}} “because, so”; {{どうして|dōshite}} and {{なんで|nande}}; {{だから|dakara}}

goal.t: 明日は早いので、今日は早く寝ます。
goal.r: Ashita wa hayai node, kyō wa hayaku nemasu.
goal.tr: I have an early start tomorrow, so I'm going to bed early tonight.

dialog.t: 明日のパーティーに来ますか。
dialog.r: Ashita no pātī ni kimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Are you coming to the party tomorrow?

dialog.t: すみません、明日は用事があるので、ちょっと…。
dialog.r: Sumimasen, ashita wa yōji ga aru node, chotto…
dialog.tr: I'm sorry, I have something on tomorrow, so…

dialog.t: そうですか。残念ですね。
dialog.r: Sō desu ka. Zannen desu ne.
dialog.tr: I see. That's a pity.

dialog.t: なんで行かないの？
dialog.r: Nande ikanai no?
dialog.tr: Why aren't you going?

dialog.t: パーティーは苦手だから。
dialog.r: Pātī wa nigate da kara.
dialog.tr: Because I'm not really into parties.

blocks.p: **Because: {{から|kara}}.** The reason comes first, then {{から|kara}}, then what follows from it: {{雨が降っていますから、タクシーで行きます|ame ga futte imasu kara, takushī de ikimasu}} “It's raining, so I'll take a taxi”. It's the reverse of English “because”: reason first, result last.

**{{ので|node}}** means the same, but sounds softer and more polite: good for excuses and requests. Before {{ので|node}}, use the plain form, and nouns and な-adjectives take {{な|na}}: {{用事があるので|yōji ga aru node}}, {{雨なので|ame na node}} “because it's raining”.

table: {{行くから|iku kara}} / {{行きますから|ikimasu kara}}

blocks.p: **Why?** {{どうして|dōshite}}, or casually {{なんで|nande}}. The answer can stop at {{から|kara}}: {{なんで来なかった？|nande konakatta?}} “Why didn't you come?” — {{忙しかったから。|isogashikatta kara.}} “Because I was busy.” And {{だから|dakara}} at the start of a sentence means “so, that's why”.

ex.t: 暑いですから、窓を開けましょうか。
ex.r: Atsui desu kara, mado o akemashō ka.
ex.tr: It's hot, so shall I open the window?

ex.t: 頭が痛いので、帰ってもいいですか。
ex.r: Atama ga itai node, kaette mo ii desu ka.
ex.tr: I have a headache, so may I go home?

ex.t: 日曜日なので、銀行は休みです。
ex.r: Nichiyōbi na node, ginkō wa yasumi desu.
ex.tr: It's Sunday, so the bank is closed.

ex.t: なんで来なかった？
ex.r: Nande konakatta?
ex.tr: Why didn't you come?

ex.t: 忙しかったから。
ex.r: Isogashikatta kara.
ex.tr: Because I was busy.

ex.t: だから、日本語を勉強しています。
ex.r: Dakara, Nihongo o benkyō shite imasu.
ex.tr: That's why I'm studying Japanese.

blocks.tip: Leaving the result unsaid is very Japanese: {{用事があるので…|yōji ga aru node…}} “I have something on, so…” is a complete, polite “no”.

mistakes.tr: It's raining, so I'm not going.
mistakes.why: A noun or な-adjective takes {{な|na}} before {{ので|node}}.

mistakes.wrong: から寒いです、コートを着ます。
mistakes.right: 寒いですから、コートを着ます。
mistakes.rw: Kara samui desu, kōto o kimasu.
mistakes.rr: Samui desu kara, kōto o kimasu.
mistakes.tr: It's cold, so I'll wear a coat.
mistakes.why: {{から|kara}} comes after the reason, not before it.

lessons.title: Explain what's going on, and ask
lessons.summary: Explain your situation, ask with concern, and lead into a request: “What's wrong?” “I have a headache.”
lessons.topic: {{～んです|… n desu}} and {{～んですか|… n desu ka}}; {{～んですが、…|… n desu ga, …}}

goal.t: すみません、道に迷ったんですが…。
goal.r: Sumimasen, michi ni mayotta n desu ga…
goal.tr: Excuse me, I'm lost… (could you help me?)

dialog.t: 顔色が悪いですね。どうしたんですか。
dialog.r: Kaoiro ga warui desu ne. Dō shita n desu ka.
dialog.tr: You look pale. What's wrong?

dialog.t: ちょっと頭が痛いんです。
dialog.r: Chotto atama ga itai n desu.
dialog.tr: I've got a bit of a headache.

dialog.t: 大丈夫ですか。薬はありますか。
dialog.r: Daijōbu desu ka. Kusuri wa arimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Are you OK? Do you have any medicine?

dialog.t: いいえ、持っていないんです。
dialog.r: Iie, motte inai n desu.
dialog.tr: No, I don't have any.

dialog.t: じゃ、私のをどうぞ。
dialog.r: Ja, watashi no o dōzo.
dialog.tr: Then have some of mine.

blocks.p: **{{んです|n desu}}: explaining.** Put {{んです|n desu}} after a plain form and the sentence becomes an explanation: not just a fact, but “the thing is…”, “you see…”. {{頭が痛いです|atama ga itai desu}} states a fact; {{頭が痛いんです|atama ga itai n desu}} explains your situation: why you look pale, why you're going home.

**Asking for the story: {{んですか|n desu ka}}.** When you notice something and want to know what's behind it: {{どうしたんですか|dō shita n desu ka}} “What's wrong? What happened?”, {{どこへ行くんですか|doko e iku n desu ka}} “Where are you off to?” (when you see someone leaving). It shows interest and concern.

**Leading into a request: {{んですが、…|n desu ga, …}}.** Explain your situation, add {{が|ga}}, and the request is understood, or follows: {{道に迷ったんですが…|michi ni mayotta n desu ga…}} “I'm lost, (could you help?)”. This is how Japanese people start most requests to strangers.

**Form.** Plain form + {{んです|n desu}}. Nouns and な-adjectives take {{な|na}}: {{学生なんです|gakusei na n desu}}, {{好きなんです|suki na n desu}}. In writing and formal speech it's {{のです|no desu}}; with friends, {{の|no}} with a rising voice asks ({{どうしたの？|dō shita no?}}) and {{んだ|n da}} explains.

table: {{行くんです|iku n desu}}, {{行ったんです|itta n desu}}
{{好きなんです|suki na n desu}}
{{試験なんです|shiken na n desu}}

ex.t: どうしたんですか。
ex.r: Dō shita n desu ka.
ex.tr: What's wrong?

ex.t: 財布をなくしたんです。
ex.r: Saifu o nakushita n desu.
ex.tr: I've lost my wallet.

ex.t: 日本の映画が好きなんです。
ex.r: Nihon no eiga ga suki na n desu.

ex.t: 明日は試験なんです。
ex.r: Ashita wa shiken na n desu.
ex.tr: I have an exam tomorrow (that's why).

ex.t: どこへ行くんですか。
ex.r: Doko e iku n desu ka.
ex.tr: Where are you off to?

blocks.tip: Use {{んです|n desu}} when there's a situation to explain. For plain facts to someone you've just met ({{アメリカ人です|Amerikajin desu}}), it would sound as if they had doubted you.

mistakes.rw: Atama ga itai na n desu.
mistakes.why: An い-adjective goes straight before {{んです|n desu}}; only nouns and な-adjectives take {{な|na}}.

mistakes.rr: Ashita wa shiken na n desu.
mistakes.why: A noun needs {{な|na}} before {{んです|n desu}}.

lessons.title: Say what you can do
lessons.summary: Talk about your abilities and what's possible, and say what your hobby is: “I can play the piano.” “You can pay by card here.”
lessons.topic: dictionary form + {{ことができます|koto ga dekimasu}}; noun + {{ができます|ga dekimasu}}; {{趣味は～ことです|shumi wa … koto desu}}

goal.t: 私はピアノを弾くことができます。
goal.r: Watashi wa piano o hiku koto ga dekimasu.
goal.tr: I can play the piano.

dialog.t: 日本語ができますか。
dialog.r: Nihongo ga dekimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Do you speak Japanese?

dialog.t: はい、少しできます。漢字も少し読むことができます。
dialog.r: Hai, sukoshi dekimasu. Kanji mo sukoshi yomu koto ga dekimasu.
dialog.tr: Yes, a little. I can read a few kanji too.

dialog.t: 車の運転ができますか。
dialog.r: Kuruma no unten ga dekimasu ka.
dialog.tr: Can you drive?

dialog.t: はい、できます。
dialog.r: Hai, dekimasu.
dialog.tr: Yes, I can.

dialog.t: 趣味は何ですか。
dialog.r: Shumi wa nan desu ka.
dialog.tr: What are your hobbies?

dialog.t: 料理をすることです。
dialog.r: Ryōri o suru koto desu.
dialog.tr: Cooking.

blocks.p: **{{できます|dekimasu}}: can.** With a noun: noun + {{が|ga}} + {{できます|dekimasu}}: {{日本語ができます|Nihongo ga dekimasu}} “I can speak Japanese”, {{テニスができます|tenisu ga dekimasu}} “I can play tennis”. As with {{好き|suki}} and {{わかります|wakarimasu}}, the thing takes {{が|ga}}.

**With a verb: dictionary form + {{ことができます|koto ga dekimasu}}.** {{こと|koto}} turns the verb into a noun, “the doing of…”, and then it works like any noun: {{泳ぐことができます|oyogu koto ga dekimasu}} “I can swim”, word for word “swimming is possible”. It also says what is possible or allowed: {{ここでカードで払うことができます|koko de kādo de harau koto ga dekimasu}} “You can pay by card here”.

table: {{漢字を読むことができます|kanji o yomu koto ga dekimasu}}
{{泳ぐことができません|oyogu koto ga dekimasen}}
{{寝ることができませんでした|neru koto ga dekimasen deshita}}

blocks.p: **Hobbies: {{趣味は～ことです|shumi wa … koto desu}}.** {{こと|koto}} again makes a verb into a noun: {{趣味は写真を撮ることです|shumi wa shashin o toru koto desu}} “My hobby is taking photos”. A shorter way to say “can” comes later ({{泳げます|oyogemasu}}); {{ことができます|koto ga dekimasu}} is always correct, if a little formal.

ex.t: 私は泳ぐことができます。
ex.r: Watashi wa oyogu koto ga dekimasu.
ex.tr: I can swim.

ex.t: 日本語が少しできます。
ex.r: Nihongo ga sukoshi dekimasu.
ex.tr: I can speak a little Japanese.

ex.t: このカードで払うことができますか。
ex.r: Kono kādo de harau koto ga dekimasu ka.
ex.tr: Can I pay with this card?

ex.t: 昨日の夜は暑くて、寝ることができませんでした。
ex.r: Kinō no yoru wa atsukute, neru koto ga dekimasen deshita.
ex.tr: It was hot last night, and I couldn't sleep.

ex.t: 図書館で本を借りることができます。
ex.r: Toshokan de hon o kariru koto ga dekimasu.
ex.tr: You can borrow books at the library.

ex.t: 趣味は映画を見ることです。
ex.r: Shumi wa eiga o miru koto desu.
ex.tr: My hobby is watching movies.

blocks.tip: If you say {{日本語ができます|Nihongo ga dekimasu}}, people will probably answer {{上手ですね|jōzu desu ne}}. Remember the modest reply: {{まだまだです|madamada desu}}.

dialog.t: すごいですね。国へは帰らないんですか。
dialog.r: Sugoi desu ne. Kuni e wa kaeranai n desu ka.
dialog.tr: Wow. Aren't you going back to your country?

dialog.t: 来月、一度帰る予定です。働く前に、家族に会いたいんです。
dialog.r: Raigetsu, ichido kaeru yotei desu. Hataraku mae ni, kazoku ni aitai n desu.
dialog.tr: I'm due to go home once next month. I want to see my family before I start work.

blocks.p: **I'm planning to…: dictionary form + {{つもりです|tsumori desu}}.** {{行くつもりです|iku tsumori desu}} “I intend to go”. For “I'm not planning to”, use the ない form: {{行かないつもりです|ikanai tsumori desu}}.

**It's scheduled: dictionary form or noun + {{予定です|yotei desu}}.** {{予定|yotei}} is for fixed plans and timetables, often decided by others: {{会議は三時に始まる予定です|kaigi wa san-ji ni hajimaru yotei desu}} “The meeting is due to start at three”. With a noun, add {{の|no}}: {{明日は出張の予定です|ashita wa shutchō no yotei desu}} “I'm due to go on a business trip tomorrow”.

**Before: dictionary form + {{前に|mae ni}}.** {{寝る前に|neru mae ni}} “before going to bed”. Even in a story about the past, the verb before {{前に|mae ni}} stays in the dictionary form: {{日本へ来る前に、日本語を勉強しました|Nihon e kuru mae ni, Nihongo o benkyō shimashita}} “Before I came to Japan, I studied Japanese”.
**After: plain past + {{後で|ato de}}.** {{仕事が終わった後で|shigoto ga owatta ato de}} “after work finishes”. It's close to て-form + {{から|kara}}, which is more common in everyday speech.

table: dictionary form + {{前に|mae ni}}: {{寝る前に|neru mae ni}}
{{の前に|no mae ni}}: {{食事の前に|shokuji no mae ni}}
plain past + {{後で|ato de}}: {{食べた後で|tabeta ato de}}
{{の後で|no ato de}}: {{授業の後で|jugyō no ato de}}

ex.t: 今年はお酒を飲まないつもりです。
ex.r: Kotoshi wa osake o nomanai tsumori desu.
ex.tr: I'm not going to drink alcohol this year.

ex.t: 飛行機は十時に着く予定です。
ex.r: Hikōki wa jū-ji ni tsuku yotei desu.
ex.tr: The plane is due to arrive at ten.

ex.t: 寝る前に、歯を磨きます。
ex.r: Neru mae ni, ha o migakimasu.
ex.tr: I brush my teeth before I go to bed.

ex.t: 仕事が終わった後で、ジムへ行きます。
ex.r: Shigoto ga owatta ato de, jimu e ikimasu.
ex.tr: I go to the gym after work.

ex.t: 授業の後で、先生に質問しました。
ex.r: Jugyō no ato de, sensei ni shitsumon shimashita.
ex.tr: After class, I asked the teacher a question.

ex.t: 日本へ来る前に、日本語を勉強しました。
ex.r: Nihon e kuru mae ni, Nihongo o benkyō shimashita.
ex.tr: I studied Japanese before I came to Japan.

blocks.tip: {{つもり|tsumori}} is for your own intentions. Asking a superior {{何をするつもりですか|nani o suru tsumori desu ka}} can sound like checking up on them; {{ご予定は？|go-yotei wa?}} “What are your plans?” is softer.

mistakes.wrong: 日本へ行きますつもりです。
mistakes.right: 日本へ行くつもりです。
mistakes.tr: I'm planning to go to Japan.
mistakes.why: Use the dictionary form before {{つもり|tsumori}}.

mistakes.right: 日本へ来る前に、日本語を勉強しました。

mistakes.wrong: 食べる後で、散歩します。
mistakes.right: 食べた後で、散歩します。
mistakes.tr: After I eat, I go for a walk.
mistakes.why: Before {{後で|ato de}}, use the plain past: {{食べた後で|tabeta ato de}}.
